passage:
Ivan chose lunch in Lisbon the way he always did: two seconds at the café counter, "the soup, please," done. Same with which tram to catch or what to wear to class. Familiar ground, small stakes; the gut was fine.
The two-year lease on the flat above the bakery was another matter. The landlord wanted a signature by the weekend, and the flat was bright and lovely. Ivan felt the pull.
Instead he printed a checklist: rent against his part-time wages, the notice period, the damp patch in the bathroom. He slept on it twice. On Saturday he showed it to Beatriz, a friend who had rented for years.
"Ask them to fix the damp in writing," she said. "And check the break clause."
Ivan did both before signing on Monday.

qa.q: What did Ivan order at the café counter?
qa.a: The soup.

qa.q: Why was Ivan happy to decide lunch in two seconds but not the lease?
qa.a: Lunch is familiar and small, so his gut is good enough; a two-year lease is big and hard to undo, so the pull of the bright flat needed checking.

qa.q: Which tools did Ivan use for the big decision?
qa.a: A printed checklist, sleeping on it twice, and advice from Beatriz, who had rented for years.

qa.q: How might the landlord see Ivan's requests?
qa.a: The landlord might find them a little fussy, but would likely see a careful tenant who will be reliable.

grounding: A young man decides everyday things by gut but uses a checklist, sleep and a friend's advice for a two-year lease.

passage:
In the university mess, Rehana picked her tray in the time it took to say "rajma rice". Same with her seat in lectures or her library corner. Small, familiar choices; no need to agonise.
Switching from engineering to design was different. One bad week in the coding lab had made her want to fill in the transfer form that same afternoon.
She didn't. She wrote a checklist instead: fees, the lost year, her portfolio, what she actually enjoyed. She slept on it for a week. Then she booked a slot with Zainab, the student advisor in the academic office.
Zainab read the list. "Is it design you want, or getting away from one bad week?"
Rehana thought. "Both, maybe. Can I sit in on a design class first?"
Zainab signed a visitor pass.

qa.q: What did Rehana want to do after the bad week in the coding lab?
qa.a: Fill in the transfer form that same afternoon.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling unsure about when Zainab asked her question?
qa.a: Whether she truly wanted design or mainly wanted to escape one bad week; she admits it might be both.

qa.q: Why did Rehana's slow approach suit this choice?
qa.a: A course switch is big and costly to undo, so a checklist, a week of sleep, advice and a trial class fit better than the quick gut she uses for lunch.

qa.q: How might Zainab view Rehana's checklist?
qa.a: Zainab probably sees a student taking a big decision seriously, which makes it easy to help with one sharp question.

grounding: A student trusts quick instinct for mess and seating choices but slows down with a checklist, sleep and advice before switching courses.

passage:
Dear Lakshmi Mashi,

You told me at the wedding to trust my gut, and I've been thinking about when that works.

For small things it's perfect. I pick my train compartment, my lunch, which assignment to do first, all by feel, and I'm usually right because I've done them a hundred times.

But the scholarship offer from Hyderabad isn't small. It means leaving Kolkata, a new language, and a bond to teach for two years afterwards. My gut screamed yes the second I read it.

So I did it the slow way. A checklist of what I'd gain and lose. Three nights' sleep. A call with a senior who took the same scholarship last year.

The answer is still yes, but now I know why, and I know about the bond.

Love,
Bidisha

qa.q: How many nights did Bidisha sleep on the scholarship decision?
qa.a: Three nights.

qa.q: Why does Bidisha trust gut feeling for lunch and train compartments?
qa.a: Bidisha has done them a hundred times, so quick feelings are usually right and little is lost if they're not.

qa.q: What did the slow way add, even though the answer stayed yes?
qa.a: It brought the two-year teaching bond into view and gave clear reasons, so the choice is made knowingly, not on excitement alone.

qa.q: How might Lakshmi Mashi feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Lakshmi Mashi might feel proud that the advice was taken thoughtfully, and reassured that such a big step was checked. 😊

grounding: A student explains using gut feeling for routine choices and a checklist, sleep and a senior's advice for a big scholarship decision.

passage: Farhan, you asked for my college radio segment, so here's my system. Amma calls me her two-second girl. Small, familiar stuff, I go with my gut. What to eat at the canteen, which shirt, which bus: two seconds, done. If it's wrong, I lose nothing. Last month was different. My department offered me a switch from mechanical engineering to product design. It was exciting, and my gut said yes, instantly. But you can't undo two years. So I slowed right down. I made a checklist: what I'd lose, what I'd gain, what the design seniors actually do all day. I slept on it three nights. I sat with two seniors and my old maths teacher. On the fourth morning I still said yes, but calmly, knowing why. I'm Ganga, and the gut still gets a vote, just not the only one on big days.

qa.q: How many nights did Ganga sleep on the decision?
qa.a: Three nights.

qa.q: Why did Ganga slow down even though her gut said yes instantly?
qa.a: She knew the switch could not be undone, so she wanted to be sure the excited feeling was backed by facts.

qa.q: Which of Ganga's steps could someone use for any big, new choice?
qa.a: Making a checklist of gains and losses, sleeping on it for a few nights, and talking to people who know that path.

qa.q: How might the design seniors have felt when Ganga came to ask questions?
qa.a: They were probably glad to help and to be taken seriously, since she wanted to know what they actually do all day.

grounding: A young adult trusts quick gut choices for small familiar matters and slows down with checklists, sleep and advice for a big one.

passage: I'm Hansa, and I've shared a flat with Arohi in Indore for a year. She's the fastest decider I know. At the tea stall she says "cutting, less sugar" before the man even looks up. She picks her kurta in the morning without opening the cupboard fully. So I was surprised last month when a colleague offered her a puppy. She didn't say yes. She wrote a list on the fridge: who walks it, who pays the vet, what happens when we travel, what the landlord says. She slept on it for a week. She called her brother, and a friend who fosters dogs. She even stood outside the building at 6 a.m. to see if she'd really get up. I don't know what she was feeling inside. But on the eighth day she said, "Not yet, maybe next year." She seemed at peace.

qa.q: What did Arohi order at the tea stall?
qa.a: "Cutting, less sugar."

qa.q: What might Arohi have been thinking when she stood outside at 6 a.m.?
qa.a: She seemed to want to test honestly whether she could keep up with a dog's needs, rather than trusting how cute the puppy felt.

qa.q: What made Arohi's approach to the puppy wise?
qa.a: She matched the effort to the stakes: quick for tea and clothes, but lists, time, advice and a real test for a big, lasting commitment.

qa.q: How does Hansa see Arohi's slow decision, given how fast Arohi usually is?
qa.a: Hansa was surprised, and could not know Arohi's inner feelings, but noticed she seemed at peace with her choice.

grounding: A flatmate watches a young adult decide small things instantly but slow down with lists, sleep and advice for a big one.

passage:
Monday. Nilesh took ten seconds to choose his canteen lunch: dosa, like always. He took thirty seconds to reply yes to a friend's movie plan. Familiar things, easy choices.
Wednesday. His senior offered him a spot in a startup: leave college after second year, work full-time. Nilesh felt a rush. He wanted to say yes on the spot. Instead he said, "Give me till Sunday." That night he made a checklist: what he'd lose, what he'd gain, what couldn't be undone. He slept on it. On Thursday he called his older cousin Damini, who had left a job to start a business, and asked her one question: "What would you check that I haven't?"
Sunday. He read his list again with a clear head. He said no to leaving, but offered to intern with the startup over the summer. They said yes.

qa.q: What did Nilesh eat for lunch on Monday?
qa.a: Dosa, like always.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh ask for time instead of saying yes to the startup on Wednesday?
qa.a: He felt a strong rush of excitement but knew leaving college would be hard to undo, so he was cautious about trusting the thrill.

qa.q: Which of Nilesh's steps would you copy for a big, new decision?
qa.a: Asking for a few days, making a checklist of what can't be undone, and getting advice from someone who has faced a similar choice.

qa.q: How might Damini feel when Nilesh asks her what she would check?
qa.a: Damini would likely feel respected and glad that Nilesh wanted her experience before a big decision.

grounding: Shows a young adult using quick intuition for familiar choices and slowing down with a checklist, sleep and advice for a big one.

passage: Seema, sit. You're choosing between two colleges, and you want me to just tell you? Let your Raghav chacha tell you how I learnt. When I was twenty, in Nagpur, I made every small choice in a snap. Which tea stall, which shirt, which bus. Mostly I was right, because I'd done those things a hundred times. Then an uncle offered me a job in Dubai, leaving right after my exams. I nearly said yes at the dinner table. My mother put her hand on mine and said, "Sleep first." I slept. I wrote a list. I talked to my professor, who had worked abroad. And I saw what I'd missed: my degree wasn't finished, the contract wasn't written, and I didn't know a single person there. I said no. Two years later I went, properly.

qa.q: Who put her hand on Raghav's at the dinner table?
qa.a: His mother.

qa.q: Why did young Raghav nearly say yes to the Dubai job at the table?
qa.a: He felt excited and was used to snap choices that usually worked for small, familiar things, so his quick instinct felt trustworthy there too.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Raghav's story, and why did it matter?
qa.a: His mother's "Sleep first" made him slow down, list the facts and ask his professor, which revealed the unfinished degree and missing contract.

qa.q: How might Raghav's mother have felt when he nearly said yes?
qa.a: She was probably worried that a big, new choice was being made in a moment of excitement, and relieved when he agreed to wait.

grounding: Illustrates, through an elder's memory, trusting quick intuition for everyday choices and slowing down with sleep, lists and advice for a big one.

passage: The storm had knocked out the hostel Wi-Fi, and Uma had until midnight to accept or decline a transfer to the new campus in another city. In the canteen, she picked her snack in two seconds: samosa, obviously. "Just accept the transfer too," said Harsha. "Go with your gut." Uma shook her head. "My gut is great at samosas. This is new, and I can't undo it." She walked to the library, which still had a line, and opened her checklist: courses, hostel, distance from home, what her professors had said. She emailed the office asking if she could reply by Friday, given the outage. They agreed. That night she slept. The next day she called her aunt and a senior who had moved. On Friday she accepted, calmly.

qa.q: What snack did Uma pick in the canteen?
qa.a: A samosa.

qa.q: Why was Uma comfortable choosing the samosa quickly but not the transfer?
qa.a: She felt confident with a familiar, small choice, but felt cautious about a new decision she couldn't undo.

qa.q: What small step helped Uma under the midnight deadline?
qa.a: She asked the office for more time because of the outage, which gave her room to sleep and seek advice.

qa.q: How might Harsha see Uma's refusal to follow her gut?

grounding: Shows a young adult trusting quick intuition for a familiar small choice and slowing down with a checklist, sleep and advice for a big one.

passage:
Tarun, twenty, worked part-time at a Bengaluru café while studying. His manager Bhupen noticed how he made decisions.

When a customer asked what tea to try, Tarun answered instantly. "Masala chai. You'll love it." He'd made that choice a thousand times.

But when Bhupen offered him a full-time job, which meant leaving his degree, Tarun said, "Can I take a week?"

"You always decide so fast," Bhupen said.

"For tea, yes. Not for this."

That week, Tarun wrote a list of pros and cons, slept on it, and talked to his professor and his older sister. He turned the job down but asked to keep his weekend shifts. Bhupen nodded, impressed.

qa.q: What did Tarun recommend to the customer?
qa.a: Masala chai.

qa.q: Why was Tarun comfortable deciding instantly about tea but not about the job?
qa.a: He felt confident about familiar, small choices, but cautious about a big, life-changing one.

qa.q: What did Tarun do during the week to decide?
qa.a: He wrote pros and cons, slept on it, and talked to his professor and sister.

qa.q: How did Bhupen see Tarun's request for a week?
qa.a: Bhupen was surprised at first but ended up impressed by Tarun's careful approach.

grounding: A young adult trusts quick intuition for familiar small choices and slows down with lists, sleep and advice for a big one.

"I always get the same thali here, Naveen. It's good. No need to think."

passage:
When I started university, I overthought everything. Which pen to buy, which canteen, which bus. It took me forever. Then, for big things, like changing my major, I just decided on a whim one night.

My friend Dilnaz pointed it out. "You spend an hour on socks and five minutes on your future."

That hurt, but she was right.

So now I have a rule for myself. Small, familiar things, I trust my gut. Pick a canteen, done. Big things, new things, things I can't undo, I slow down: I make a list, sleep on it, and ask someone I trust.

Last month I was offered a semester abroad. I took two weeks, talked to my parents and my advisor, and said yes. I'm Samir, and I haven't regretted it.

qa.q: What was Samir offered last month?
qa.a: A semester abroad.

qa.q: How did Samir feel when Dilnaz pointed out the problem?
qa.a: Samir felt stung and hurt at first, but saw she was right.

qa.q: What system does Samir now use for decisions?
qa.a: Trust the gut for small, familiar things; for big, new or irreversible ones, make a list, sleep on it and ask someone trusted.

qa.q: How might Dilnaz feel seeing Samir's new approach?
qa.a: Dilnaz probably feels glad that her honest comment helped Samir change.

grounding: A young adult learns to use quick intuition for small familiar choices and slow thinking for big, irreversible ones.

passage:
In her mother's tailoring shop in the small town, Bhavna matched thread colours without thinking. A customer held up a peacock-blue blouse piece, and Bhavna's hand went straight to the right spool. "That one," she said, and she was right, as usual.
But when a letter came offering her a seat in a two-year design course in Pune, far from home, she didn't trust the rush of "yes!" in her chest.
That night she wrote a list: fees, hostel, who would help Amma in the shop, what the course's past students were doing now. She slept on it. The next day she called her old teacher, and asked Ritu, who had studied in Pune, about the hostel and the classes.
Ritu laughed. "You pick thread in one second, but this takes a week?"
"Thread I can change tomorrow," Bhavna said. "This I can't."

qa.q: Where is the design course Bhavna was offered?
qa.a: In Pune.

qa.q: Why didn't Bhavna trust the rush of "yes!" in her chest?
qa.a: She felt excited, but she was cautious because the move was big, new and hard to undo, unlike choosing thread.

qa.q: What steps did Bhavna use for the big decision?
qa.a: She wrote a list, slept on it, then asked her old teacher and Ritu for advice.

qa.q: How does Ritu see Bhavna's two ways of deciding?
qa.a: Ritu finds it funny at first that thread takes one second and the course takes a week, until Bhavna points out the difference in stakes.

grounding: Shows a young adult trusting quick intuition for familiar small choices and slowing down with a list, sleep and advice for a big new one.
